Spotify connection setup (once)

Spotify only hands your playlist list to apps registered with them. It's free and takes a minute. Go to developer.spotify.com/dashboard, then Create app, tick Web API, and paste this as the Redirect URI: . Then copy the app's Client ID here.

Add a song, album or playlist link, or share it straight from the YouTube, YouTube Music, Spotify or SoundCloud app to Omega System. Play it here, tap Sample, and tap again to stop. The take lands in Chop. On a computer, Chrome asks to share this tab: tick Also share tab audio. On the phone it records through the mic, so turn the volume up, or plug a cable from the headphone out into a USB audio input. Spotify plays 30-second previews until you log in below. WhoSampled looks up what the song samples and who sampled it.

Presets
Foot switches
Variables box

Modeled from the Taurus Model 205A schematic: the fixed presets use the original resistor values for the contours, filter offset and oscillator mix. Variable unlocks the Variables box. The foot sliders open the filter and set the level, like the pedals.

Accent and Slide latch on and apply to the notes you play and record. Notes played hard (top of the pad, or high MPC/keyboard velocity) are accented too, and a note that starts while the previous one is still held slides into it, like a tie on the 303. Repeated accents with high resonance build up the squeal, as on the original.

Modeled on the Rev 3 Prophet-5: two CEM3340 oscillators, CEM3320 four-pole filter, two CEM3310 envelopes per voice, five voices. Knobs step in 128 increments like the original (pitch and cutoff move in semitones). Vintage sets how much the five voices differ and drift.

The 128 General MIDI instruments, grouped by family. ◀ ▶ step through them and play each one. MIDI files that pick an instrument (program change) switch this automatically.

The keys play this pad's sample at every pitch. C3 is its own pitch. Uses the pad's start/end, loop, reverse and level.

Modeled on the Oberheim OB-Xa: two CEM3340 oscillators with sync, a CEM3320 filter you can switch between the 2-pole response (the open, brassy Oberheim sound) and 4-pole, two ADSRs, an LFO with sample & hold, and eight voices spread across the stereo field like the OB-Xa's pan pots. Programs are in the style of famous OB-Xa and OB-X parts.

Each model runs its own circuit: Roland's IR3109 filter (Juno-60, SH-101, JX-3P), the Moog ladder (Minimoog), the Curtis chip (Six-Trak) or the CS-80's high-pass + low-pass pair with touch-sensitive brilliance. DCO models stay locked in tune; the Minimoog, SH-101 and CS-80 drift like real VCOs.

CASIOCZ-101PHASE DISTORTION

Phase distortion: a cosine read through a bent phase. DCW depth and its envelope sweep from a pure sine to saw, square, pulse, double sine or the resonant waves; two lines can be layered, detuned, ring- or noise-modulated.

Plays one sound up and down the keys at the machine's own quality: the SK-1 squashes it to 8-bit at 9.38 kHz with no smoothing (the crunchy toy sound); the Emax to 12-bit at 27.7 kHz through its analog filter. Use a built-in tone, any pad's sound or a file.

commodore128SOUND INTERFACE DEVICE · MOS 6581

The SID chip as the C128 had it: three voices, each a 24-bit oscillator at 1.0227 MHz with triangle, saw, pulse and noise (switch on several for the SID's combined waves), ring mod and sync, the chip's own envelope timing (the decay steps and the "ADSR bug" included) and the 6581's gritty filter. Poly plays three notes at once; Mono stacks all three voices on one note, and Arpeggio cycles held notes at 60 Hz like C64 music. The C128 presets are BASIC 7.0's built-in ENVELOPE 0–9.

RolandD-50LINEAR SYNTHESIZER

LA synthesis: each tone has two partials joined by one of the D-50's 7 structures (S = synth: saw or square through the resonant TVF; P = PCM attack or loop; ring = ring modulation). Upper and Lower tones play whole, dual or split, then the chorus and reverb. The PCM attacks here are synthesized, not Roland's samples.

PPGWAVE 2.2

Two digital oscillators per voice read 8-bit, 128-sample waves from 64-wave tables (stepped like the hardware; the top four waves are triangle, pulse, square and saw), swept by envelope 3, the LFO and the wheel, then a resonant 24 dB analog-style filter. 30 original wavetables.

YAMAHADX1DIGITAL PROGRAMMABLE ALGORITHM SYNTHESIZER

Two DX7 voices per note (Dual), split across the keyboard (Split), or one (Single), like the DX1. Load .syx takes DX7 32-voice banks and single voices (also DX7II / TX802 / TX7 / DX7-compatible files). The sound is modeled on the chips: the OPS runs at 49,096 Hz with log-sine and exponential ROMs and 14-bit operators, the EGS envelopes step in 0.023 dB units, and the output goes through the floating-point 12-bit DAC and the 16 kHz filter. Editing voice A here changes this track's copy only.

ARPOMNI-2POLYPHONIC SYNTHESIZER

Built from the Omni-2 service manual: 500 kHz master oscillator and top-octave divider, differentiated-square "sawtooth" (Hollow lets the negative spike through), a 22 µF keying capacitor per key, three bucket-brigade "phasers" on the strings, the ARP 4075 24 dB filter with an RC ADSR on the synth, and low-note-priority bass on the lowest 20 keys. Fully polyphonic like the real one: every key sounds from one divide-down tone generator. Strings have their own crescendo and sustain. The Synth section sends all notes through one resonant 4-pole filter and one ADSR, as the Omni-2 does, so a new key re-triggers the sweep. Keys below the split play the Bass section. Chorus and Phaser are on the panel.

Bass section
Strings and brass

Modeled from the Solina schematics: divide-down tone with the original sawtooth shaping, per-key sustain, one shared crescendo, and the three-line ensemble driven by its chorus and tremolo oscillators. Notes below C3 also play the mono bass section. Viola is the 8' rank and Violin the 4' rank.

Getting started

The Omega System is a small studio for your phone: an MPC-style drum rack, synths, audio tracks you record from a USB-C interface, a mixer with effects, patterns for song parts, and export to WAV, MP3, stems and MIDI.

Install it like an app

  1. Android: open the app in Chrome, tap Chrome's ⋮ menu, then Add to Home screen. iPhone: open it in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen.
  2. Open it from the home screen icon. It runs full-screen and works offline after the first visit (MP3 export needs internet the first time).

Your first beat in a minute

  1. On Drums, tap pads to hear the built-in kit.
  2. Tap Overdub (or the round record button at the top). You get a one-bar count-in, then the loop plays.
  3. Play pads in time. Each pass layers on top. Tap ■ to stop.
  4. Made a mistake? Undo removes the last pass.

Everything saves automatically on this phone. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Transport, tempo and the record button
  • ▶ / ■ starts and stops. The space bar does the same on a keyboard.
  • ● Record depends on the tab: on Audio it records the armed audio track; everywhere else it toggles drum and synth Overdub.
  • Position shows bar.beat.sixteenth. During a count-in it shows “In 1… In 4”.
  • BPM: type a value, use − / +, or tap Tap three or more times in tempo. Range 40–240.
  • Loop: 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars for the current pattern.
  • Click turns the metronome on during playback. The count-in always clicks.
  • Count-in can be turned off in Setup → Recording. Click level there goes up to 400 %: past 100 % the click drives a clipper, so it gets much louder and harder, for loud rooms and headphones.

When the clock is set to Follow MPC (Setup → MIDI), the tempo controls lock and play/stop come from your MPC.

Drums: real-time recording
  • Pads are laid out like an MPC: A01 bottom-left, A16 top-right. A dot means the pad has hits in this loop.
  • Overdub: play pads while the loop runs and they are recorded. Each pass layers on top.
  • Timing (timing correct): Off keeps hits exactly as played; 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 and triplets snap hits as you play. Apply snaps hits you already recorded.
  • Swing delays every second 1/16 (0–60%). It applies to hits that sit on the 1/16 grid.
  • Note repeat: turn it on, then hold a pad. It retriggers at the Repeat rate in time with the loop; with Overdub on, the repeats are recorded.
  • Erase: turn it on, then hold a pad while the loop plays. Its hits disappear as the playhead passes them.
  • Velocity: Full level plays every hit at full volume. By touch height makes hits louder the higher you strike the pad. Phones can't sense pressure.
  • Timeline: shows every pad's hits across the loop. Tap a hit to delete it, or tap a row to select that pad.
  • Undo steps back through recording passes and edits. Double loop doubles the loop length and copies the hits so you can add variations. Clear all (tap twice) empties the pattern's drum hits.

If recorded hits land a little late, raise Setup → Recording → Pad timing. It compensates for touchscreen delay.

Pads and samples
  • Load file puts a WAV, AIFF, MP3, FLAC or OGG file on the selected pad. The file name becomes the pad name.
  • Sample input records from your USB-C interface onto the pad: tap to start, tap again to stop. Silence at the start is trimmed and the level is normalized.
  • Built-in puts the current kit's sound back on the pad.
  • Chop opens the selected pad's sample in the Chop tab.
  • Level, Tune (±24 semitones), Pan and Decay (shortens the sound) work per pad.
  • Mute grp: pads in the same group cut each other off, like closed and open hi-hats.
  • Clear hits (tap twice) removes only the selected pad's hits.
Loading sounds onto pads
  • Edit (above the pads): turn it on, then tap a pad for its menu: Delete sound (the pad goes empty; its hits stay but play nothing), Delete sound and its hits, Load…, or Built-in sound, or Clear all pads… (also the Clear all button above the pads, and in Pad sound). Turn Edit off to play the pads again.: empty every pad, empty every pad and its hits, or reset all 16 to the built-in sounds.
  • Load… in a pad's hold menu, or Load file in Pad sound, opens the sample browser. Tap a sound to hear it, then use ◀ ▶ to step through the folder; each one plays as you land on it (the next few are loaded ahead, so it's instant). Load on pad keeps the one you like. Switch Tap: hear to Tap: load if you'd rather every tap go straight onto the pad. Search looks through your whole samples folder, subfolders included, e.g. "909 snare". My folder remembers your folder and where you were in it; Recent keeps every sample you've loaded. With a keyboard: ↑ ↓ to step, Space to hear, Enter to load.
  • Catalog sorts every sound in your samples folder into categories by its name and folder: Kicks, Snares, Claps, Hats, Cymbals, Toms, Percussion, 808 & Bass, Vocals, FX, Synth & Keys, Loops, Breaks, Other. Tap a category chip to browse just those. All lengths / One-shots / Loops filters by length, and loops show their BPM when it's in the file name. Pick a sound to see its tools: ☆ makes it a favorite (favorites get their own chip and sit at the top), the category menu moves it (or makes a New category…), and tags (e.g. "dusty, 90s, SP") are searchable. Added new files to the folder? Tap Rescan. Your favorites, categories and tags are kept.
  • Load files onto pads (above the pads): pick a whole sample pack at once. Each file goes to the pad its name matches (kick/BD, snare/SD, clap, rim, closed/open hat, ride, crash, low/mid/high tom, conga, cowbell and so on). Files that match nothing fill the remaining pads in order.
  • Built-in (in Pad sound) puts the pad's original sound back.
FX sends and returns
  • Every effect has a return strip on the Mixer, between the tracks and Master: Reverb, Delay, and each FX rack unit you send to. Tap + Returns to show all of them. Each return has a level fader, pan, mute, solo and meter. EDIT / UNIT jumps to that effect's settings.
  • Faders menu (top of the Mixer): choose Send → Reverb, Send → Delay or a rack unit, and the track faders turn amber and set how much of each track goes to that effect. Choose Volume to go back.
  • Send faders and return levels can be MIDI-learned and automated like any fader.
Pad sampler: start, end, loop, ADSR, filter

In Pad sound (with SP-1200 mode off). The waveform shows the start and end points and the loop point.

  • Start / End trim the sample. Reverse plays it backwards.
  • Loop repeats the part between Loop from and End for as long as the note lasts. Held live, it loops while you hold the pad; in the sequencer it loops for the recorded note length, or until the pad is hit again.
  • One shot / Hold: One shot plays the whole sample on each hit. Hold plays only while you hold the pad, then goes into Release, and recorded notes keep the length you held them.
  • Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release: a volume envelope for each pad. Length still shortens the sound like before.
  • Filter / Reso: a low-pass filter for each pad.
Oberheim OB-Xa

Choose Oberheim OB-Xa in the synth's instrument menu. Two oscillators per voice (saw and pulse, sync, osc 2 detune), a filter that switches between 2-pole (the open, brassy Oberheim sound) and 4-pole, filter and loudness ADSRs, an LFO with sine, square and sample & hold, filter envelope to osc 2 for sync sweeps, and eight voices spread across the stereo field. Unison stacks all eight with detune.

Programs in the style of famous OB-Xa and OB-X parts: Jump Brass, 1999 Stab, Separate Ways, Purple Pad, Tom Sawyer Growl, Mr. Roboto Brass, Oberheim Strings, plus Sync Sweep, S&H Bubbles, Unison Bass, Brass Swell, Poly Sweep, Bell Keys and Electro Lead. They're starting points modeled on those records, not copies of factory patches.

Tempo detection
  • Every loop or longer sample gets its tempo found automatically. One-shots (under about a second) have none.
  • Pads (Pad sound): shows e.g. "97 BPM · 2 bars". Set project changes the project tempo to the sample's. Fit to … speeds or slows the sample to the project tempo; like an MPC or SP-1200, the pitch moves with it. Detect runs it again.
  • Sample browser: the tempo shows next to the name while you preview. In Catalog, Tempos finds the tempo of every sound in your folder in the background (tap it again to stop), and you can search by tempo, e.g. "93bpm".
  • Audio tracks: imported loops get their length in bars from the detected tempo, then follow the project tempo.
  • Loops trimmed to a whole number of beats give an exact tempo. Untrimmed audio is fine too, just less exact. A "~" means the beat was hard to find.
Arpeggiator

On the Synth tab, above the keys. Each synth has its own settings.

  • Arp on: hold notes on the grid, the keyboard or your MIDI keyboard, and the arp plays them one at a time. While the beat plays it locks to the tempo and grid. When stopped it runs on its own at the project tempo.
  • Pattern: Up, Down, Up-down, Down-up, As played (the order you pressed), Random, or Chord (all notes together, rhythmically).
  • Rate: 1/4, 1/8, 1/8T, 1/16, 1/16T, 1/32. Octaves: repeats the pattern 1–4 octaves up.
  • Gate: how long each note sounds. Swing: pushes every other note late.
  • Latch: the notes keep going after you let go. Play a new chord to replace them; Clear stops them.
  • Press record while the arp plays and its notes are written into the pattern.
Synth tracks

The tabs at the top of the Synth screen are your synth tracks (up to 4). + adds one. Press and hold a tab to rename it, duplicate it, or delete it.

Vinyl & tape noise

Mixer → FX on any track (or Master) → Vinyl & tape. Pick Sound like (Dusty 45, Worn LP, Thrift-store record, Cassette, Hiss only) or set Crackle, Hiss, Pops and Rumble yourself. Blend sets how loud the noise sits under the sound. On a track, the noise follows the sound, so it's baked in like a sample off a record. On Master you can choose whether it plays with the sound or all the time.

Akai S950 voice

Pad sound → S950 rate plays the pad as 12-bit at an S950 sample rate (48, 40, 32, 31.25, 22.05, 15 or 7.5 kHz), with no smoothing between samples, so lower rates get the gritty S950/S900 sound. S950 filter (0–99, like the S950's FILTER value) is a steep 6-pole low-pass with no resonance, modeled on the switched-capacitor filter design in the S900/S950 family. It's built from the published design and specs, not a trace of a real unit.

MPC: line up, import, export
  • Setup → MIDI → Pad notes → MPC: pads 1–16 (Bank A) on any MPC, including the MPC Sample, Live, One, X, Key, Force, 1000, 2500 and 60, play A01–A16 here, and MIDI files go both ways on the same notes.
  • Import files… (Setup → Export, or Pads → Sequencer → Import…): pick an MPC drum program (.xpm) together with its samples and they land on the right pads with their level, pan and tuning. Also MPC1000/2500 .pgm, MPC2000 .snd samples, a project's .xpm/.wav files (and the .xpj for its tempo), ZIP packs, MIDI, and audio in WAV, AIFF, MP3, FLAC, OGG, M4A or Opus. If you set a samples folder, missing samples are found there.
  • Export: MPC kit (pad WAVs + .xpm program + MIDI on MPC notes), Every pad, exploded (one file per pad), Every track (stems), the full mix, or MIDI.
General MIDI sounds

Synth → Sound → instrument General MIDI (128 sounds): all 128 GM instruments (pianos, organs, guitars, basses, strings, brass, reeds, flutes, synth leads and pads, ethnic, percussion, effects), grouped by family. ◀ ▶ steps through them. Imported MIDI files that choose instruments switch to them automatically, and a program change from your MPC picks the sound. These are synthesized approximations, built for a light phone app, not sampled GM sounds.

MIDI files

Import MIDI (Pads → Sequencer, or Setup → Export) puts a .mid file into the current pattern: drums (channel 10) onto the pads, matched by note (your A01 note setting, or General MIDI drum names), and each other channel onto a synth track (up to 4). The pattern becomes 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars to fit, and the tempo is taken from the file. Undo takes it back. Export MIDI saves the pattern or song as a .mid for the MPC or any DAW.

16 Levels, Erase, Repeat
  • 16 Lvl: tap a pad, then 16 Lvl. Every pad now plays that sound at a different pitch (A09 is its own pitch, one semitone per pad, A01 = −8 … A16 = +7). Record it like normal pads. Tap 16 Lvl again to go back.
  • Keys: on the Synth tab, Sound → instrument Pad sample (keys) plays any pad's sample across the keyboard (C3 = its own pitch).
  • Erase: turn it on, then tap a pad to delete its hits in this pattern. Undo brings them back.
  • Repeat: while playing, tap a pad to start repeating it, tap again to stop. No holding needed.
▶ Hear on every page

Each page that makes sound has a green ▶ Hear (or ▶ Play) button at the top. Pad sound plays the pad. Sound plays a chord on the synth. Arp plays a chord through the arpeggiator. Speech and Vocoder say your line. Effects and FX rack play a short beat through the effects. Sequencer, Notes, Patterns and Song start and stop the beat. Turntable starts and stops the record, and Sampler and Chop play the sound.

All stop

Double-tap the play/stop button to stop every sound. The red ■ ALL button at the top stops everything at once: the beat, every pad (including looping and held ones), every synth note and the arpeggiator, both turntables, the sampler, sample previews and the reverb/delay/FX tails. It also sends "all notes off" to your MPC or other MIDI gear. It can be MIDI-learned to a pad or button, and Esc on a keyboard does the same.

Bluetooth headphones

Bluetooth adds about 150–250 ms of delay, and phones often don't report it. In Setup → Performance, turn Bluetooth headphones on and tap Measure with your headphones on. Tap the button on each of the 12 clicks, and the app sets the offset for you, or set the BT offset slider yourself. Recorded pads, keys and audio then land where you heard them. The playhead, pad lights and MIDI clock to the MPC also line up with what you hear. Turn it off when you switch back to wired, USB or the phone speaker.

Screens without scrolling

Each tab fits on the screen. Tap a section title (▸) and it opens over the screen like an MPC page; if it has more than fits, flip pages with ◀ ▶ at the top or swipe left and right. ✕ closes it. Smaller parts inside a section fold open and shut.

SP-1200 mode

Turn on SP-1200 mode in the pad card and the whole drum rack runs through a model of the E-mu SP-1200's audio path:

  • Samples are converted like the original: a 7th-order anti-alias filter, sample-and-hold at 26,041.67 Hz (20 MHz ÷ 768) and a truncating 12-bit converter, up to 65,536 samples (about 2.5 s) per sound.
  • Pitch uses drop-sample playback with E-mu's semitone table and a 7-bit fraction counter, including its slight detuning. Range is −16 to +15 semitones, and +12 and up all play at double speed, like the hardware.
  • An 8-bit level DAC sets each hit's volume, and each of the 8 output channels is mono: a new hit on a channel cuts the one before.
  • SP output (per pad): 1–2 go through an SSM2044-style 4-pole transistor-ladder filter that opens on each hit and closes over about a quarter second; 3–6 each have their own fixed low-pass (3 is darkest, 6 is brightest); 7–8 are unfiltered.
  • Dyn cutoff and Dyn reso set where the outputs 1–2 filter settles and how much it resonates, like the sliders on the Rossum reissue.

Tips: put kicks and bass sounds on 1–2 for that filtered thump, snares on 3–4, hats on 7–8. Tune samples down and play them back for the classic gritty sound.

Any track can also get the 12-bit, 26 kHz grit without the rest: Mixer → FX → 12-bit 26k.

The filter data comes from libmd12 (see Credits), which was checked against circuit simulation and a real SP-12. Above about 12 kHz this app's filters cut a few dB more than the analog originals.

Chop: slice samples across pads
  1. Get a sample: Load file, Record (from the input), From pad (the selected pad), or From track (any audio track's clip, including stems).
  2. Slice it: Equal cuts 2–16 even slices; Transients cuts at hits, use Sensitivity for more or fewer; Manual lets you Split the selected slice or Remove its marker.
  3. Adjust: drag a marker by its triangle, or nudge the selected slice's start by ±1 or ±10 ms. Tap a slice or its number to hear it. Slice points snap to zero crossings so they don't click.
  4. Send to pads: pick the first pad; slices fill the following pads (up to 16). This replaces those pads' samples.

Make a pattern writes hits that play the slices back in their original timing, so a chopped break plays as the full loop. Set how many bars the sample is and tap Set BPM to match the tempo to it.

Audio tracks and recording

Set up your interface

  1. Plug your USB-C interface into the phone.
  2. Tap Enable input (Audio tab or Setup) and allow the microphone when Chrome asks.
  3. If it doesn't pick the interface, choose it under Setup → Audio input → Device.
  4. Choose Channels: input 1, input 2, or both as stereo.

Play through the MPC (or any USB device)

With the MPC plugged in by USB-C, pick it under Setup → Audio input → Sound out. If it isn't listed, tap Enable input first so the phone lists your USB devices. Android usually switches to a USB audio device by itself; if the sound stays on the phone, swipe down from the top of the screen, tap the media output button and pick the MPC. The MPC's speaker or headphone output then plays everything in the app.

Record

  • Arm the track to record (only one at a time) and choose its Record length (1–8 bars).
  • Press ●. From stop you get a one-bar count-in; while playing, recording starts at the next loop.
  • Monitor plays the input through the armed track's effects. Use headphones to avoid feedback.
  • Recordings are shifted automatically to allow for the phone's audio delay (latency). If takes land late, turn Setup → Recording → Auto off and raise Offset; if they land early, lower it. Record claps along with the click to check.

Import, warp and clips

  • Import loads an audio file into the track and guesses its bar length from the tempo. Fix it with Clip if the guess is wrong.
  • Clips remember their tempo and follow the project BPM with Warp: Complex stretches without changing pitch (best for vocals and instruments); Beats retriggers each 1/16 (best for drum loops); Re-Pitch speeds up and slows down like a record; Off plays as is.
  • Stems splits the clip into four tracks (see Stem separation).
  • Up to 10 audio tracks. Clips belong to the current pattern.
Stem separation

Tap Stems on an audio track with a clip. It splits the clip into Drums, Bass, Vocals and Other as four new tracks that stay in time with the song, and mutes the original. The four stems add up exactly to the original, so nothing is lost.

How it works: the sound is analysed in short slices; steady tones are separated from hits by median filtering, the low steady part becomes Bass, and the steady part in the middle of the stereo image (150 Hz–7 kHz) becomes Vocals.

  • Works best on full stereo mixes with the vocal in the centre. On a mono file, everything steady in the vocal range ends up in Vocals.
  • Expect rougher results than AI tools such as Ableton 12.3's stem separation, which use large neural networks that don't fit in a phone browser.
  • Clips up to 2 minutes. It runs in the background so the app stays responsive.
  • Load the Drums stem into Chop (From track) to chop a break out of a song.
Instrument tracks and the note grid
  • Up to 4 instrument tracks. Tap + at the top of the Synth tab to add one; new tracks start as a Prophet-5.
  • Each track can be a Prophet-5, Solina strings, TB-303 or Moog Taurus: pick it from the menu next to the track name. Each has its own section in this help.
  • The grid only plays notes in the chosen key and scale. Each row is a fourth higher than the one below, like Ableton Push. Orange pads are the root note. Use Oct − / + to move up and down. Choose Chromatic for every note.
  • Keyboard swaps the grid for a piano keyboard of 1, 1½ or 2 octaves starting at C. It plays every note; keys outside the key are shaded and the root notes have an orange dot. Play chords with several fingers, or slide along the keys to play each one in turn. Lower on a key plays louder, unless Full level is on. Oct − / + shifts it.
  • Overdub records what you play, with the same Timing (timing correct) as the drums.
  • Piano roll shows the notes in this pattern. Tap a note to delete it, or tap an empty spot to hear that pitch. Undo and Clear work as on the drums.
  • A MIDI keyboard or your MPC can play a track: set Setup → MIDI → Notes play to it.
Solina strings

Any synth track can be a Solina String Ensemble: on the Synth tab, change Synth to Solina strings. It is modeled from the original Solina schematics.

  • Tone: all notes come from one divide-down tone generator, so octaves are phase-locked and each note has the tiny detune of a real top-octave generator chip. Each square wave is shaped by the original capacitor-diode circuit into the slightly hollow Solina sawtooth.
  • Viola plays the 8' rank (as written), Violin the 4' rank (an octave up). Use both for the classic sound.
  • Trumpet and Horn send the tone through the formant circuit for brassy colours.
  • Cello (8') and Contrabass (16') are the mono bass section: the lowest note you hold below C3 plays it, through its own low-pass.
  • Crescendo is one shared swell: the sound fades in when you start playing from silence, and legato notes join without restarting it, like the original's single VCA.
  • Sustain lets each key ring on after release; the slider sets how long (the value shown is the circuit's time constant).
  • Ensemble is the famous three-line chorus: three delay lines around 2.8 ms, swept 120° apart by the slow chorus oscillator (about 0.75 Hz) plus the faster tremolo (about 6.3 Hz). Turn it off to hear the raw organ-like tone. Wide spreads the three lines left, centre and right instead of the original mono.
  • Chorus Hz and Tremolo Hz are the trimmers inside the original; Ens depth and Tremolo set how strong each sweep is.

Try it through the Vocoder for the late-70s string-vocoder sound.

Prophet-5

Any synth track can be a Prophet-5: on the Synth tab, change Synth to Prophet-5. It is modeled on the Rev 3 instrument from Sequential's service and owner's manuals, with five voices.

  • Oscillator A: saw and/or pulse (width 1–99%), and Sync to Oscillator B. Frequency steps in semitones over four octaves.
  • Oscillator B: saw, triangle and/or pulse, Fine (up to a semitone up), Lo freq turns it into an LFO (0.4–30 Hz), and Kbd off makes it a drone.
  • Mixer: levels of A, B and white noise into the filter. Turn them up for a hotter, more saturated filter.
  • Filter: the CEM3320 four-pole low-pass. Resonance self-oscillates above about 7. Keyboard makes the cutoff follow the notes, so a self-oscillating filter can be played in tune.
  • Envelopes: filter and amplifier ADSR, about 1 ms to 30 s; the knob is exponential (5 is about half a second). Release off gives a short click-free release.
  • Poly-Mod: the filter envelope and Oscillator B modulate Oscillator A's pitch, pulse width and/or the filter, separately in every voice. Oscillator B into Freq A gives clangy FM bells; the filter envelope into Freq A with Sync on gives the classic sync sweep.
  • LFO and Wheel-Mod: the LFO (0.04–20 Hz, saw/triangle/square) and pink noise, mixed by Source mix, reach the destinations you switch on, with depth set by the Mod wheel. A MIDI keyboard's mod wheel and pitch bend work when Setup → MIDI → Notes play is set to this track.
  • Unison stacks all five voices on the lowest note held, with Glide. Vintage sets how much the five voices differ and drift, like real component tolerances; 0 is perfectly matched.

Like the original, most knobs move in 128 steps, so cutoff and pitch change in semitone steps. Programs give you starting points: Brass, Poly strings, Sync lead, Unison bass, Poly-mod bell, Pad, Pluck and Resonant sweep.

TB-303

Any synth track can be a TB-303 bass line: on the Synth tab, change Synth to TB-303. It follows the stock 303 as documented by Robin Whittle (Devil Fish) and published analyses of its diode-ladder filter.

  • Saw / Square: the square is made from the saw by a transistor shaper, as on the original, so it is not a perfect square.
  • Cutoff, Resonance, Env mod, Decay (200 ms–2 s filter envelope) and Accent work like the 303's knobs. The filter does not follow the keyboard and rings hard at high resonance but never self-oscillates, like a stock unit.
  • Accent: notes played hard (top of the pad, or high velocity from the MPC or a keyboard), or any note while the Accent latch is on, are accented: louder, brighter, with the envelope forced to 200 ms. With resonance up, a run of accents builds up the squeal, because the accent circuit's capacitor keeps some charge between notes.
  • Slide: a note that starts while the previous one is still held glides into it over the 303's 60 ms without restarting the envelopes. The Slide latch makes every note you play or record slide.
  • Notes keep their accent and slide when recorded with Overdub, so patterns play back with the same squelch.
  • For a classic acid line: Saw, Cutoff around 400–600 Hz, Resonance 7–9, Env mod 5–7, Decay low, Accent high, then add the Mixer's Saturator.
Moog Taurus

Any synth track can be a Moog Taurus bass pedal: on the Synth tab, change Synth to Moog Taurus. It is modeled from the Taurus I (Model 205A) owner's & service manual and schematic. It is monophonic and plays the lowest note held, like the pedals.

  • Presets: Taurus (both oscillators in unison, slow swell, big filter sweep and long decay), Tuba (second oscillator an octave up, gentle filter), Bass (punchy, steady filter) and Variable, which opens the Variables box. The fixed presets use the original resistor values for their envelopes, filter offset and oscillator mix.
  • Foot switches: Octave moves from 16' up to 8'; Glide slides between notes (time set by the Glide slider, up to 0.5 s); Decay lets notes ring out after release, otherwise they stop quickly.
  • Foot filter opens the filter up to 3 octaves and Foot volume sets the level, like the two foot sliders. Beat detunes the second oscillator up to 2% for the classic chorusing; Tune covers ±8%.
  • Variables box (Variable preset): octave Lo/Med/Hi, Osc B frequency (198–484 Hz), B-mix-A, Cut-off (7 octaves from 40 Hz), Emphasis (self-oscillates from about 8), Contour amount (up to 7 octaves), filter attack 5–56 ms and decay 50 ms–2.8 s, loudness attack 5–560 ms, decay 50 ms–2.8 s and sustain.

Tip: the Taurus preset with Decay on and the foot filter around half way is the classic huge pedal tone. Play it from the low octave of the grid or route your MPC or a keyboard to it.

Star Screamer 350 vocoder

The vocoder makes a synth “talk”: your voice shapes the synth's sound. It is modeled on the Roland SVC-350's circuit from its 1979 service notes.

  1. On the Synth tab, turn Vocoder on. That synth becomes the instrument.
  2. Voice: Live input uses your USB-C mic; or pick an audio track with a recorded vocal (mute that track in the mixer if you only want the vocoder).
  3. Hold chords on the grid (or your keyboard/MPC) and talk or sing.
  • 11 sliders: the original frequency section, 10 bands (about 160 Hz to 5 kHz) plus HF, the high consonant filter that lets “s” and “t” through.
  • Balance: from vocoder only to dry voice.
  • Harmonics: brightness of the instrument going in. Brighter, buzzier synths (saw waves) are more understandable.
  • Ensemble: the original stereo chorus.
  • Hold: press and hold to freeze the last vowel, like the footswitch.

The vocoder is silent when no instrument is playing. The original's sound detector does the same, so breathing and room noise don't leak through.

Carrier, growl and presets

  • Carrier: the vocoder normally plays from this track's own synth. Pick another synth track to use its sound instead (for example a TB-303 or Taurus line), and mute that track in the mixer if you only want the robot.
  • Growl: the buzzy, gritty low end of early-80s electro vocals. It adds a square wave one octave below the carrier (a flip-flop divider, like an octave pedal) and overdrives the carrier before the filter bank, keeping the same loudness.
  • Presets: SVC-350 clean, Electro growl, Space robot, Egypt robot, Jet robot (bright), Metal monster, and Change the Beat ('fresh'). That last one sets up a deep, slow talking-machine line, "Ahhhh, this stuff is really fresh", feeds it to the vocoder and holds a low note under it.

Speech (talking machine)

  • Type lines in the Speech box, one per line. Preview plays the raw voice. Send to vocoder builds a muted Speech audio track from the lines and sets it as this vocoder's voice. If the carrier synth has no notes, a held low note is added so it talks straight away; play or record your own notes to change the pitch.
  • Voice: Robot (monotone), Deep, Normal or High. Pitch and Speed fine-tune it. Timing: each line starts on its own bar, or lines run back to back.
  • It's a formant synthesizer with English pronunciation rules, like the early-80s talking chips. Spell a word your own way if it comes out wrong, or type phonemes between slashes: /F R EH SH/. Repeating a vowel stretches it ("Ahhhh", "freeesh").

The Star Screamer 350 panel

  • The panel follows the Roland SVC-350's front: black rack panel, red and white lettering, and boxed sections. INPUT has MIC (the voice), INSTRUMENT (the carrier synth) and the INST LEVEL switch (−30, −15, 0 dB). FREQUENCY has the 11 band sliders, BALANCE and MASTER VOLUME. VOICE CHARACTER has HARMONICS, GROWL and S/T NOISE. REMOTE has VOCODER/DIRECT, HOLD and ENSEMBLE.
  • Knobs: drag up or down to turn them, or tap the red value under a knob to pick a setting from the menu.
  • S/T NOISE: when the voice is mostly hiss (S, T, SH, F), white noise replaces the carrier, so consonants stay crisp instead of turning into notes.
  • PROGRAM presets: Jonzun Crew, Newcleus, Egyptian Lover, Starscream, Mr. Roboto, Cylon Warrior, Fresh (Change the Beat), Herbie Hancock, and Clean SVC. Each one sets the panel, switches the carrier to a Prophet-5 on its "Vocoder carrier" program (bright saw and pulse, filter open), writes a speech line and holds a carrier note. These are in the style of those records, not copies of them.
Mixer and effects
  • Each strip has pan, a fader with meter (double-tap to reset), Mute and Solo. FX opens the track's effects below.
  • Effects run in this order: Vocoder (synths) → Saturator → Redux → EQ Three → Auto Filter → Chorus → Compressor → Sidechain duck → Pan/Auto Pan → Fader → Sends.
  • EQ Three: low, mid and high, ±15 dB. Auto Filter: low-, high- or band-pass with cutoff and resonance.
  • Saturator adds warm drive. Redux crushes bits and sample rate. 12-bit 26k sets Redux to the SP-1200's exact rate and depth.
  • Chorus widens. Auto Pan moves the sound left and right at a tempo-synced rate.
  • Sidechain duck: the track dips each time the chosen pad hits (usually the kick). Release sets how fast it comes back.
  • Compressor evens out the level. At 0% it is fully bypassed.
  • Sends go to the shared Reverb and Delay. Set their size, time and feedback on the Master strip.
  • Sends to the FX rack feed the five rack units below the mixer (see FX rack).
  • Master EQ (Master strip → FX): low cut, plus ±12 dB at 80 Hz, 200 Hz, 500 Hz, 1.2 kHz, 3 kHz, 6 kHz and 12 kHz. It's switched out when flat.
  • EQ match works on anything: the master (Master strip → FX), every track (its FX page) and both turntable decks (Wheel tab, under the mixer). Pick a Reference: a song file on your phone, the master mix, any track, or a deck. Then tap Match: the app compares the two average spectra in 31 bands (1/3 octave) and sets a matching EQ, up to ±9 dB. Amount sets how much to use; the graph shows the reference (blue), this sound (white) and the correction (orange). Match again after big changes. A matched track only uses CPU for its EQ while a match is on.
  • Bus compressor (Master strip → FX), in the style of the SSL G-series quad bus compressor: THRESHOLD, RATIO 2:1 / 4:1 / 10:1, ATTACK 0.1–30 ms, RELEASE 0.1–1.2 s or AUTO (fast after short peaks, slower when squeezing hard), MAKE-UP, a sidechain high-pass so the kick doesn't pump the mix, and MIX for parallel compression. The GR meter shows gain reduction. Presets cover mix-bus glue, hip-hop bus, drum smash, punch, pumping and more.
  • CLIP lights: each mixer channel has a CLIP light that turns red when the channel goes over full scale (the master checks before its limiter). A flashing CLIP badge in the top bar shows it on any page; tap it to go to the mixer. Tap a CLIP light to clear it.
  • Master: Glue compression (adds 6 ms of latency while on, so leave it off while recording live) and a soft clipper that stops harsh overs.
FX rack

Below the mixer is a rack of five classic studio units. Each one is a shared send effect: turn up a track's Sends to the FX rack slider (Mixer → FX on that strip) to feed it. Every unit has a Presets menu, its own menus, and knobs. A unit nothing is sent to uses no CPU.

  • Lexicon PrimeTime (Model 93): two delays, A on the left and B on the right, each up to 128 ms × Multiply. As on the original, a bigger multiplier gives longer delays but less bandwidth (×1 12 kHz, ×2 6 kHz, ×4 3 kHz, ×8 1.5 kHz). A time/B time can follow the tempo (dotted 1/8 for that "Sucker MC's" exit), and Multiply rises automatically if a synced time needs it. Recirc feeds back through the High cut filter, normal or inverted. The VCO sweeps the delay over 2:1 for flanging and chorus.
  • Deltalab Effectron (ADM 1024): a 1-bit adaptive delta-modulation delay. Pick a Range (flange, double, short or long echo). The longer the delay inside a range, the slower the coder runs and the grittier it gets. ADM grit adds more. Pan puts the copy in the centre, to one side (Haas: about 22 ms on the right makes a vocal wide without an echo), or as the wide stereo-simulation pair. Regen can be negative (inverted phase).
  • Eventide H910 Harmonizer: one side is pitched up and the other down by Detune cents, each with its own delay up to 112.5 ms. ±9 cents at 15/25 ms is the classic doubled-vocal wall. Raw splicing keeps the H910's audible splice clicks and compander pumping; Smooth is the later de-glitched sound. Feedback goes past 100% like the original.
  • MXR 113: a 10-bit digital delay inside a compander. Bandwidth trades tone for time (20 kHz up to 160 ms … 2.5 kHz up to 1.28 s), so long repeats get darker and grainier. Regen at 100% holds the repeats.
  • Lexicon 224 / AMS RMX16: 224 programs (Vocal Plate, Percussion Plate, Concert Hall, Room, Chamber) run at the 224's narrow ~8 kHz bandwidth with its 12-bit grain. The RMX16 programs are full-bandwidth: Plate A1, Hall C1, Ambience, Nonlin 2 (the gated snare: holds, then stops dead) and Reverse 1 (builds up, then stops). Size sets the decay time or gate length, and Treble sets how fast the highs die.
The Wheel of Steel (two decks, DJ mixer)

The Wheel tab is a two-deck DJ setup in the style of Serato DJ: the waveforms of both decks on top (title, artist, time left, BPM and key over each), two turntables in the style of the Technics SL-1200 MK2 with the mixer between them (HI / MID / LOW, filter, channel faders, level meters and the crossfader), and the library with crates underneath. Touch a record to scratch it. Each turntable has Start · Stop, 33 / 45, pitch (double-tap to zero), Cue, Sync and Load. Tap a deck to make it the one Deck controls works on (hot cues, loops, rolls, FX, key lock, nudge, censor, MIDI platter).

Serato compatible: tracks keep what Serato DJ saved in them: hot cues (with their colours), saved loops, the beatgrid, BPM, key, title and artist, from MP3, AIFF, WAV and FLAC (◆ marks a track with Serato data). Serato crate imports .crate files from your Serato folder (Music/_Serato_/Subcrates); tracks already in the library join the crate, and the rest join when you add their files. Make your own crates with + Crate and the ⋮ menu on each track.

Waveforms

  • Each deck has a scrolling waveform (6 seconds around the playhead) coloured like Serato's: red for lows, green for mids, blue for highs, with the beat grid (bright lines on every bar) and hot cues and loops marked. Under it, the whole-track overview shows where you are.
  • BPM and the first beat are detected when you load a track. The readout shows the BPM as played (with pitch) and time remaining.

Deck controls

  • Start · Stop, 33/45, Pitch with range ±8 / ±16 / ±50 %, and Nudge (hold to push the deck 4 % faster or slower for a moment).
  • CUE: while stopped, sets the cue point where the record is; while playing, jumps back to it and stops.
  • SYNC matches this deck's tempo to the other deck and lines up the beats. While Sync is lit, it follows tempo changes on the other deck. Touch the pitch to drop out of Sync.
  • SLIP: scratches, loops and the like play over the top while the track keeps running underneath; when you let go it carries on from where it would have been.
  • CENSOR (hold): plays backwards, then drops back in where the track would have been.
  • Performance pads: HOT CUES (8 coloured cues: tap an empty pad to set, a lit one to jump; Delete cue then a pad clears it), AUTO LOOP (1/8 to 16 beats, starting on the beat; tap again to exit) and ROLL (1/32 to 4 beats while held; the track picks up where it would have been).
  • Loops: IN and OUT set a loop by hand; RELOOP/EXIT, ½ and ×2.
  • Cut (hold) mutes the deck while held.
  • Scratch by putting your finger on the record. Load record loads a track (up to 15 minutes) onto the deck on screen; each deck keeps its track.

Mixer and crossfader

  • Each channel has HI, MID and LOW (down to KILL), a FILTER knob (left = low-pass, right = high-pass, middle = off) and a channel fader.
  • The crossfader has three curves: Scratch (sharp cut: fully open a hair past the edge, for cuts and transforms), Smooth (for mixing) and Linear. REV flips it (hamster style). It reacts in about 1–2 ms, fast enough for cuts.
  • To cut from your MPC or another controller: Setup → MIDI learn, tap the crossfader, move a knob or fader on the controller, Done.

MIDI

  • Everything here can be MIDI-learned: the crossfader, channel faders and EQ knobs, Start, CUE, SYNC, SLIP, the 8 pads (they work as hold buttons for rolls), Censor, Nudge and Cut. Buttons act on the deck on screen; map DECK 1 / DECK 2 to switch.
  • MIDI platter (Denon DN-S3700 or any jog wheel), per deck: put the DN-S3700 in MIDI mode and choose it in Setup → MIDI. Pick the deck, tap Learn platter, start the DN-S3700's platter (motor on, 33 RPM) and let it spin for 3 seconds. The app works out which message the platter sends and how many steps make one turn, then turns on Platter control: the record follows your platter exactly, one real turn is one turn on screen. REV flips the direction; Steps / turn fine-tunes the speed.
  • A MIDI knob mapped to the platter (tap the platter while learning) also scratches: full knob travel is two turns.
  • Both decks play into the master, so the master EQ, CLIP lights and limiter apply.
Automation
  1. On the Mixer tab, turn on Automate (it turns red).
  2. Press play and move any fader, pan, EQ, filter cutoff/resonance or send. The moves are recorded into the loop.
  3. Turn Automate off. The moves play back every pass.
  • Touching an automated control while not recording takes it over by hand. Re-enable automation hands it back.
  • Each track's FX panel lists its automation with a small graph and Clear.
  • Automation belongs to the pattern, so each pattern can have its own sweeps. It is included in exports.
Patterns and Song mode
  • A pattern holds its own drum hits, synth notes, audio clips, automation and loop length. Pads, samples, synth sounds and the mixer are shared.
  • Pattern buttons sit above the drum pads. + copies the current pattern so you can make a variation.
  • Tap a pattern while playing and it starts at the next bar, or at the end of the loop if you set Launch that way (Song tab).
  • On the Song tab you can rename patterns, change their length and delete them.
  • Song: add parts (pattern × repeats), reorder with ↑, then turn Song on and press play. It plays the parts in order and stops at the end. Export renders the whole song.
MIDI and syncing with your MPC
  1. Connect the MPC to the phone with a USB-C cable, or through a USB MIDI interface.
  2. Setup → MIDI sync → Connect MIDI, and allow it when Chrome asks. The app picks the MPC under From and To; choose it if not.
  • Follow MPC: press play on the MPC and this app starts with it, at its tempo, and stops with it. On the MPC, turn on sending MIDI clock (and start/stop) in its MIDI or sync settings.
  • Lead MPC: this app sends tempo, start and stop. On the MPC, turn on receiving MIDI clock.
  • Offset: if the two sound out of step, move it until the kicks line up. Positive delays this app.
  • Play these pads from the MPC's pads: MPC pads trigger the app's pads, with velocity, and are recorded with Overdub. Note repeat and erase work too.
  • A01 note / Learn: select A01 on the Drums tab, tap Learn, then hit the MPC pad that should play it. The rest follow in order.
  • Notes play: send incoming notes to the drum pads or to a synth (for a MIDI keyboard). Channel filters which MIDI channel is listened to.

MIDI learn (map MPC knobs and pads to any control):

  1. Setup → MIDI sync → MIDI learn. An orange bar appears, and every control you can map gets a dashed outline.
  2. Go to any tab and tap a slider, menu, number box or button. It gets a white outline.
  3. Move a knob on the MPC (or hit a pad). That control now follows it, and turns green.
  4. Map as many as you like, then tap Done.
  • Knobs move sliders across their full range, step through menus, and press buttons when turned past halfway. Pads press buttons (Play, Overdub, Mute…), step a menu to its next choice, or flip a slider between its lowest and highest setting.
  • Mapped controls work from any tab, even when that page isn't open. Moving a mapped track control while Automate is on records automation.
  • A note you map to a control no longer plays a pad. Mapping the same knob again moves it to the new control.
  • Your mappings are listed under MIDI learn. Remove one with ✕, or use Clear all mappings. They are saved with the project.
Exporting: WAV, MP3, stems and MIDI
  • Full mix: everything you hear, as one file.
  • Every track (ZIP): the mix plus each track rendered on its own through its effects and sends (muted tracks are skipped). All files are the same length so they line up from bar 1 in any DAW or on the MPC.
  • MIDI file: drum hits on channel 10 (A01 = the A01 note set in MIDI settings, C1 by default) and each synth on its own channel, at the project tempo with swing applied.
  • Format: WAV 16-bit, WAV 24-bit (best for further mixing), MP3 320 or 192 kbps. Rate: 44.1 or 48 kHz.
  • Repeat: how many times to loop the current pattern. With Song mode on, the whole song is exported instead.
  • Files go to your Downloads folder. Share sends the last export straight to another app (Drive, WhatsApp, a DAW…).
Look

The app is styled after the Akai MPC60 (warm-grey case, blue backlit display with white lettering, dark rubber pads, mode keys with red LEDs) and the E-mu SP-1200 (charcoal panel, white silkscreen, slider faders). Settings work like the MPC's: − and + step a value (hold to scroll), and the value itself is a drop-down to jump straight to a setting.

Saving, updates and storage
  • The project, samples and recordings save automatically in this browser on this phone. Nothing is uploaded.
  • Clearing Chrome's site data for this app, or uninstalling Chrome, deletes the project. Export anything you want to keep.
  • Commodore 128 (Synth → Instruments): the SID chip, three voices with triangle / saw / pulse / noise, ring mod, sync, the chip's envelopes and gritty 6581 filter; Poly, Mono (stacked) and 60 Hz Arpeggio. Presets include the C128 BASIC 7.0 instruments.
  • Roland D-50: LA synthesis with 7 structures of PCM attack and synth partials, Upper / Lower tones (whole, dual, split), chorus and reverb.
  • PPG Wave 2.2: 8-bit wavetables (30 tables, 64 waves each) swept by envelope 3, the LFO and wheel, through a 24 dB filter. The display shows the table.
  • Juno-60, SH-101, JX-3P, Minimoog, Six-Trak, CS-80 (Synth → instrument): analog models, each with its own oscillators, filter type (Roland IR3109, Moog ladder, Curtis, Yamaha high + low-pass), envelopes and presets. Juno chorus I / II / I+II.
  • Casio CZ-101: phase distortion, 8 waves, two lines (1, 2, 1+1′, 1+2′) with DCW and DCA envelopes, ring and noise mod.
  • Casio SK-1 and E-mu Emax: samplers at the machines' rates and bit depths (8-bit 9.4 kHz / 12-bit 27.8 kHz). Play a built-in tone, a pad's sound, or load a file. The Emax adds its 4-pole filter and envelopes.
  • DR-110, DMX, Synsonics (Pads): step grids like the machines. Load their sounds onto the pads, tap the grid to program, Accent for loud hits.
  • Sidechain (FX → Duck): pick any track or the drums as the key; the track ducks whenever the key plays.
  • Microverb (FX rack): the Alesis Microverb's 16 programs (halls, rooms, plates, gated, reverse).
  • Resonance tamer + clipper (FX → Master): finds harsh peaks and turns them down as they happen; the clipper adds drive and holds a ceiling.
  • SP-1200 (Pads → SP-1200): the E-mu faceplate: SP mode, banks A / B, eight faders for Tune, Decay or Mix, and eight pads.
  • Ensoniq DP/4 (FX rack): four effect units (reverbs, chorus, flanger, phaser, delays, pitch shift, distortion, rotary, sweep filter) in Parallel, Series or 2 × 2, with presets. Send any track to it with its DP/4 send.
  • Yamaha DX1 (Synth → instrument): two DX7 voices played Single, Dual (layered, B detuned) or Split. Load .syx (or Import) takes DX7 32-voice banks and single voices. Modeled on the DX7 chips: 49,096 Hz operator chip with log-sine and exponential ROMs, 14-bit operators, the EGS envelope, 32 algorithms, the floating-point 12-bit DAC and 16 kHz output filter. Edit the algorithm, feedback and each operator's level, ratio and decay.
  • ARP Omni-2 (Synth → instrument): built from the service manual. Strings: Violin 4′, Viola 8′, and single-note Cello 8′ / Bass 16′ on the lowest 20 keys, through three bucket-brigade “phasers” and a shared attack. Synthesizer: 4′ / 8′ through the ARP 4075 24 dB filter with an ADSR, LFO, Single trigger. Bass Voices 8′ / 16′ with Staccato. Hollow changes the waveform; Chorus Phaser sends the synth through the string phasers.
  • FX (top bar, every screen): opens the effects for what you're on: the drums on Pads, the synth on Synth, the track on Audio. Tabs switch to any track, the Master or the FX rack. The button lights up when that track has effects patched in.
  • FIRE (top bar): the machine fries. Smoke pours out, the sound overdrives, crushes and cuts out, and the settings slowly mangle themselves, more the longer it burns. Everything that comes out is recorded: switch it off and your settings come back, and the fried take is in Chop (ready to slice onto the pads) and your sample bin. Press play first so there is a beat to burn.
  • Packs (Pad sound → Save pack / Load pack): a .omegapack file with all 16 pad sounds, every pad setting, and the Chop sample with its slice points.
  • TV and game controllers: on Google TV install the Android app; the remote's arrows move and OK presses, Back closes pages. Any game controller works on every device: Select switches MENU (D-pad moves, A presses, B back, LB / RB change page, X all stop) and PLAY (16 buttons play the pads or synth notes, triggers by how hard you pull). Start plays and stops.
  • Mixer: channel faders start at −20 dB (double-tap a fader to go back to −20 dB), leaving headroom.
  • Projects (Setup): Save keeps the project in your list. Open switches projects. Export makes a .omega file to move it to another device. New project (tap twice) saves the current one first, then starts fresh.
  • Updates arrive automatically. If something looks old, close the app fully and open it again.
Troubleshooting
No sound
Tap any pad once: phones only start audio after a touch. Check the phone isn't on silent and the Master fader is up. If a track is soloed (S lit), only soloed tracks play.
The interface or mic isn't found
Unplug and replug it, then tap Enable input again. Check Chrome has microphone permission (lock icon in the address bar → Permissions). Some interfaces need to be plugged in before the app opens.
Recordings or pads are out of time (latency)
For audio takes, adjust Setup → Recording → Offset. For pad hits, raise Pad timing. Turn off master Glue while recording to save 6 ms.
MIDI device doesn't show up
Tap Refresh MIDI devices. Make sure the MPC's USB mode allows MIDI and the cable carries data (some charge-only cables don't).
The MPC and app drift apart
Only one device should send clock. Use Follow MPC or Lead MPC, not both, and make sure the MPC isn't also receiving clock from somewhere else.
Crackles or dropouts
Go to Setup → Performance → Audio buffer and choose Medium or Large. This is the biggest fix. Also close other apps and turn off battery saver. The Prophet-5 and Solina use the most power when many notes are held, and very long Complex-warped clips at odd tempos add load too. An effect set to zero is switched off completely, so it costs nothing.
MP3 export fails
The MP3 encoder downloads the first time you use it. Connect to the internet once, or export WAV.
“Could not read that file”
Use WAV, AIFF, MP3, FLAC or OGG. Some phone voice-recorder formats aren't supported.
Workflow tips
  • Build a beat in Pattern 1, tap + to copy it, then strip it down for a verse or add hats for the hook.
  • Record with Timing Off for feel, then Apply 1/16 to individual takes if they need tightening.
  • Chop a stem: Stems → Chop → From track → Transients → Send to pads with Make a pattern on, then replay it your own way.
  • Duck pads and bass from the kick (Sidechain duck, 40–60%) for a pumping mix.
  • Export Every track as WAV 24-bit to finish a song in another DAW or load parts into your MPC.

Connect your MPC with a USB-C cable (or a USB MIDI interface), then tap Connect MIDI.

Follow MPC: press play on the MPC and this app starts with it, at its tempo. Lead MPC: this app sends tempo, start and stop, so set the MPC to receive MIDI clock. If the two sound out of step, move Offset until the kicks line up.

Bluetooth adds about 150–250 ms that the phone often doesn't report. Turn this on and set the offset (or tap Measure with your headphones on) so recorded pads, keys and audio, the playhead and MIDI sync line up with what you hear. It doesn't make the sound itself come sooner; wired or USB is still the fastest for playing live.

If the sound crackles or drops out when a lot is playing, choose a bigger buffer. A bigger buffer adds a little delay between tapping a pad and hearing it. The app reopens to apply the change, and your project is kept.

Offset is for audio takes. Pad timing makes up for touchscreen delay when you record pads. If your hits land late, raise it.

If recordings land late, raise the offset. If they land early, lower it. Record a few claps along with the click to check.

Export

Import takes MIDI (.mid), MPC drum programs (.xpm with their WAVs, MPC1000/2500 .pgm), MPC2000 .snd, MPC projects (.xpj: tempo), ZIP packs, and audio: WAV, AIFF, MP3, FLAC, OGG, M4A/AAC, Opus. Pick several at once: a program and its samples, or a whole kit.

Files go to your Downloads folder. Share sends the last export to another app.

Projects

v103

Everything also saves automatically as you work. Save keeps this project, its sounds and recordings, in your list so you can come back to it. Opening another project or starting a new one saves the current one first, so nothing is lost. Your sample library and SoundFonts are shared by all projects. A project file (.omega) moves a project to another phone, tablet or computer.
